newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Sundays - April 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Sundays - April 20.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
SUNDAY TELEGRAPH
-- CO-OP DEMANDS CAYMANS PROBE

The Co-operative Wholesale Society has called for an investigation into a 2m stg payment to Trellis International by prospective bidder Andrew Regan, made when he bought the Co-op's food manufacturing business two years ago. The Co-op wants Regan's adviser Hambros to find out if Allan Green, the society's retailing controller, had any interest in the payment.
-- RJB HIT BY POWERGEN CHEAP COAL CONTRACTS

The electricity generator PowerGen has signed contracts with Midlands Mining and Mining Scotland for between a third and a half of its coal needs from next year. RJB Mining has to renegotiate its coal contracts in 1998.
-- STANDARD LIFE TO LAUNCH OWN BANK

Standard Life is expected to reveal plans for a new banking operation this week to rival the one launched by the Prudential. The insurance group will offer a range of products and services including a savings facility.
-- CORDIANT SET FOR THREE-WAY SPLIT

Advertising group Cordiant is set to announce a flotation of its two main agency networks, Saatchi & Saatchi and Bates Worldwide, to raise 300m stg. The dramatic corporate restructuring has been organised by bankers SBC Warburg.
-- BASS FAVOURITE FOR WILLIAM HILL

Troubled leisure group Brent Walker is expected to announce plans to float its betting shop chain William Hill this week. However, it is rumoured that rival Bass, with its Coral chain of bookmakers, is working on a take-over plan.
THE OBSERVER
-- CWS PROBES CAYMAN ISLANDS DEAL

Businessman Andrew Regan has been forced to shelve plans to break up the Co-operative Wholesale Society after the suspension of two Co-operative executives last week and the announcement of secret payments to a mysterious Cayman Island company.
-- SIEMENS WARNS UK NOT TO SPURN EMU

The chief executive of Siemens UK, Jurgen Gehrels, has warned that thousands of jobs and valuable inward investment could be lost if Britain decides to reject European monetary union. Gehrels said that major companies need exchange rate stability.
-- MORGAN GRENFELL BIDS FOR AUSTRALIAN FUND MANAGER

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell is understood to have bid for Australian fund management business Axiom which looks after funds for the New South Wales government. However, close observers believe the National Australia Bank will clinch the deal for Axiom.
-- FRAUD INQUIRY AS NAMES CRY FOUL

The Metropolitan Police is investigating the sale of up to 200m stg worth of Norwich Union guarantees to Lloyds Names during the 1980s which allowed Names to increase underwriting capacity. The allegations is that they were mis-sold guarantees by independent financial advisers.
-- SEARS SET TO SELL FREEMANS FOR 375M STG

Retailing group Sears is set to sell its mail order business Freemans to Littlewoods this week for around 375m stg. City analysts believe the deal will be approved by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission with few changes.
MAIL ON SUNDAY
-- ICI'S 4BN STG BID IN UNILEVER SALE

ICI has launched a 4bn stg bid for most of Unilever's speciality chemical businesses. The units were put on sale last month as part of a radical shake-up of the group by Unilever's boss Nial Fitz-Gerald.
-- 6M STG FOR THE RIGHT
BOSS AT CO-OP

Business Andrew Regan is thought to have approached at least one supermarket chief executive with a lucrative financial proposal to join him in his bid for the Co-operative Wholesale Society. However, merchant bank Hambro are under pressure to resign as his adviser after serious allegations made against him by CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth.
-- CRISIS-HIT HELENE ON THE BRINK

Troubled clothing supplier Helene announced last week that it expects to lose its Stock Exchange listing due to the forced winding-up of several key subsidiaries after a deal with German retailer Dyckhoff fell through. Angry shareholders are expected to demand more information about the group's finances this week.
-- BOSSES IN THE FIRING LINE

The Securities and Investments Board wants to change the rules and force senior managers to justify their behaviour and competence in the event of a serious failure. Next month's discussion paper will also call for senior managers to ensure that controls are in place to prevent financial disasters.
-- LABOUR'S PENSION PLEDGE

Shadow Treasury spokesman Mike O'Brien has announced a Labour government would force pension giants to compensate half a million victims of the mis-selling scandal within a year. It would also strengthen the Securities and Investments Board, allowing it to impose fines and penalties on companies which did not co-operate.
SUNDAY TIMES
-- ALLIED IRISH AND SAINSBURY QUEUE FOR SHARE OF CO-OP

Allied Irish Banks and J Sainsbury are rumoured to be interested in the Co-operative Wholesale Society, if the bid by Andrew Regan's Galileo Group succeeds. The news will strengthen the hand of Regan who has already assembled a powerful team of City backers.
-- CORDIANT POISED TO ANNOUNCE BREAK-UP PLANS

Advertising group Cordiant is expected to announce plans to break-up tomorrow offering investors shares in its two advertising networks Saatchi & Saatchi Advertising Worldwide and Bates Worldwide. Bankers SBC Warburg believe a demerger is the best way to unlock the value in the company.
-- AMERICAN EYES BATTERSEA DEAL

American businessman Steve Roth has spoken to property company Parkview about the possibility of an equity stake in London's Battersea power station. He wants to inject up to 200m stg into the project to help transform the derelict site into a leisure and retail complex.
-- CONSUMER SPENDING WILL BOOM AFTER THE ELECTION

The Chartered Institute of Marketing is predicting a mini- boom in consumer spending after the general election fuelled by windfall gains from building society conversions and an end to the political uncertainty. The CIM survey believes sales volume will increase by 5.3 percent this year.
-- PRICE WAR PUSHES DIRECT LINE INTO LOSS

The pioneering telephone-based insurer Direct Line is expected to announce a loss when its parent company, Royal Bank of Scotland, reveals its interim profits next month. Profits have been hit by intense competition, an increase in personal injury payouts and a tough winter.
INDEPENDENT ON SUNDAY
-- CO-OP PUTS HEAT ON REGAN

The Co-operative Wholesale Society is to investigate a significant payment by Hobson, Andrew Regan's previous business vehicle, to an offshore company made when the CWS sold its former food manufacturing businesses in 1994.
-- 700m STG DOWN THE TUNNEL

Shareholders are expecting bad news when Eurotunnel announces its results for 1996 this week. The results are likely to be overshadowed by a new debt restructuring agreement and the fire safety report. Shareholder activist group Adacte will renew its demand for French bankruptcy proceedings to be started against the company.
-- TOBACCO'S TOUGH FUTURE

The Labour party is expected to ban all tobacco advertising to discourage young people from smoking if elected. Britain's tobacco companies, Imperial Tobacco and Gallagher, are facing an uncertain future with recent legal action in America which could intensify in the UK under a Labour government.
-- US MAD COW FEARS

Cattle and grain futures plunged last week after the death of an American farmer from Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. The Food and Drug Administration has speeded up its deliberation on how to prevent BSE hurting US cattle herds. Last year the UK government linked CJD with eating BSE-infected beef.
-- ROUX IN PENSION APPEAL

Restaurateur Michael Roux has decided to appeal against an Inland Revenue charge of 400,000 stg on his pension imposed by the High Court earlier this month. Ian Altug of accountants Hacker Young, said he had acted in good faith.
